title: Play (III.31–III.34)
hookLine: the season's over and fun feels like slacking; an old story about an apostle and a bird says otherwise
tomorrow: a thought you never asked for shows up. is that already a sin?

lines: NO GAME, FIRST TIME IN MONTHS.
cards: Saturday morning, and for the first time in months there's no game. The cleats sit by the door. The group chat says pickup at the park, just for fun, and a voice in your head says fun is for people with nothing due.
A very old story answers that voice. An old man sits stroking a partridge in his hands. A hunter walks by and stares: is this really John, the apostle, passing his time with a bird?
John looks at the bow on the hunter's shoulder, and asks him a question.

teach.b: Do you keep that bow bent all the time? No, says the hunter, or it would lose its spring. Then don't be surprised, John answers, if the mind needs a little rest too.

Francis de Sales tells this story, from the old writer Cassian, in his chapters on recreation, and he means it plainly. Sometimes, he says, we have to relax the mind and the body. That isn't a lapse in devotion.
It's part of keeping a person whole.
Then he names good kinds: a walk in the open air, cheerful conversation, music, games where skill decides who wins. Then the measure.

Recreation is meant to refresh, so don't let it eat up the time or the heart. Play, but not so attached that you can't put it down. And the games he's wary of: ones where chance alone decides and money rides on it.
Even dances, which in his day could run long and loose, he doesn't simply ban; he asks when, why and how much.
Here's one to tell a friend tonight: a book about the devout life spends whole chapters defending games. Under all of it is John's bow. The slack is what lets it spring back.

how: Catholic parishes host picnics, festivals and sports, and the Church keeps Sunday as a day of worship and rest.

o: rest that refreshes the mind and body
competing hard to prove who's the best
wasting time that should go to prayer

p: loses its spring if always bent
walks, talk, music, games of skill
chance alone, with money riding on it

s: a devout life, for Francis de Sales, means giving up games
he says mind and body need recreation, and he names good kinds.
the partridge story comes from Cassian, retold by Francis
a bow kept always bent loses its spring.
he's wary of it, but he asks when, why and how much.

games.q: your little brother is in three leagues and a summer camp, and he's stopped laughing at practice. what would Francis's chapter ask first?
o: is any of it still refreshing him, or only using him up?
they're games of skill, not chance, so isn't it all fine?
shouldn't he drop sports altogether and just rest?
games.why: skill games are on Francis's good list, but recreation is meant to refresh. once it eats the time and the heart, it has lost its point.

practice: Play something for these two minutes, just for the joy of it: toss a balled-up sock from hand to hand, hum a song you loved as a kid, doodle in a margin. Nothing to win, nothing to post.
If you pray, you can thank God for rest when you stop.

wordCard.voice: Play. Recreation that refreshes body and mind, taken freely and in measure, like a bow let slack so it keeps its spring.

carryVoice: Keep this one: play is good, even for an apostle with a bird in his hands. See you tomorrow.
